Part I

High Level

Foundations · architecture and workflows

1.Foundations

1.1Introduction

A Kubernetes Service is a core API object (v1/Service, maintained by the Kubernetes project's SIG Network) that gives a changing group of pods one stable DNS name and virtual IP and spreads connections across the Ready ones. It has no binary of its own: the API server stores it, controllers keep its endpoint list current, kube-proxy on every node enforces it in the kernel and CoreDNS publishes its name. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller adds cloud load balancers for type: LoadBalancer.

✓ It is

  • a stable name + virtual IP for a set of pods
  • label-based membership that follows scaling and rollouts
  • per-connection load balancing across Ready pods
  • four types: ClusterIP · NodePort · LoadBalancer · ExternalName (+ Headless)

✕ It is not

  • a process or pod you can exec into
  • an L7 router (host/path rules are Ingress / Gateway API)
  • per-request load balancing or retries (a service mesh does that)
  • a firewall (that is NetworkPolicy)

Definitions

Service

What it isA namespaced API object that gives a set of pods one stable name and address.
🎯 Why it existsPods are replaced all the time; callers need something that does not change.
📄 What it looks like
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-api-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: menu-api
⚙ What Kubernetes doesAllocates a ClusterIP, keeps an EndpointSlice up to date, programs every node, publishes DNS. Before: 10.244.1.20 hard-coded → After: menu-api-service.
📍 Where it livesjahez-prod, in etcd; enforced by rules on every node
⚠ Watch outIt is not a proxy process and not a load-balancer pod — there is nothing to "restart".

Labels & selector

What it isA selector is a set of labels; every Ready pod that has all of them is a backend.
🎯 Why it existsMembership must follow pods automatically as they scale and move.
📄 What it looks like
selector:
  app: menu-api
⚙ What Kubernetes doesThe EndpointSlice controller re-evaluates it continuously. Before: 3 pods → After scaling: 8 endpoints, no edit.
📍 Where it livesService spec.selector ↔ pod metadata.labels
⚠ Watch outOne typo = zero endpoints and "connection refused".

ClusterIP (virtual IP)

What it isA virtual IP from the service range that exists only as kernel rules.
🎯 Why it existsClients need one address that survives every pod change.
📄 What it looks like
clusterIP: 10.96.0.50   # allocated
⚙ What Kubernetes doesReserved on create, never changes while the Service exists. Before: pod IP churn → After: 10.96.0.50 forever.
📍 Where it livesservice CIDR 10.96.0.0/12; no network card has it
⚠ Watch outImmutable: delete + recreate gives a new IP. You cannot ping it.

EndpointSlice

What it isThe live list of pod IP:ports behind a Service, with ready / serving / terminating flags.
🎯 Why it existsSomething has to track which pods exist and are healthy right now.
📄 What it looks like
endpoints:
  - addresses: ["10.244.1.20"]
    conditions: {ready: true}
⚙ What Kubernetes doesWritten by the EndpointSlice controller from selector + readiness. Before: 3 ready → after a failing probe: 2 ready.
📍 Where it livesdiscovery.k8s.io/v1, owned by the Service
⚠ Watch outEmpty slice is the #1 reason a Service "does not work".

kube-proxy

What it isA DaemonSet that turns Services + EndpointSlices into iptables / nftables rules on every node.
🎯 Why it existsThe virtual IP needs to be translated to a pod IP on whichever node the caller runs.
📄 What it looks like
-A KUBE-SVC-MENU … -j KUBE-SEP-…
-j DNAT --to-destination 10.244.2.20:8080
⚙ What Kubernetes doesWatches the API and syncs rules within about a second. Before: packet to 10.96.0.50 → After DNAT: 10.244.2.20:8080.
📍 Where it livesevery node (kube-system)
⚠ Watch outIt balances per new connection, not per request.

Cluster DNS record

What it isCoreDNS answers <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local for every Service.
🎯 Why it existsApps should use names, not IPs.
📄 What it looks like
menu-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local
  → A 10.96.0.50
⚙ What Kubernetes doesWatches Services; A record for ClusterIP, pod IPs for Headless, CNAME for ExternalName.
📍 Where it livesCoreDNS pods behind the kube-dns Service (10.96.0.10)
⚠ Watch outShort names only work inside the same namespace.

port · targetPort

What it isport is what clients dial on the Service; targetPort is where it lands on the pod.
🎯 Why it existsClient ports should not depend on container ports.
📄 What it looks like
ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: http
⚙ What Kubernetes doesDNAT rewrites :80 to the pod's port. Before: callers know 8080 → After: callers use 80.
📍 Where it livesService spec.ports[]
⚠ Watch outSwapping the two is a classic CKAD mistake.

NodePort

What it isA Service type that also opens one port (30000–32767) on every node.
🎯 Why it existsReach a Service from outside without a cloud LB.
📄 What it looks like
type: NodePort
ports:
  - port: 80
    nodePort: 30080
⚙ What Kubernetes doeskube-proxy matches the port on every node and forwards to any pod. Before: unreachable → After: node-IP:30080.
📍 Where it livesevery node's kernel
⚠ Watch outNo health checks; high ports in URLs; open on all nodes.

LoadBalancer

What it isA Service type that also asks a controller for a cloud load balancer.
🎯 Why it existsOne stable, health-checked public address.
📄 What it looks like
type: LoadBalancer
loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.io/nlb
⚙ What Kubernetes doesAWS Load Balancer Controller creates an NLB and writes its hostname to status. Before: <pending> → After: k8s-…elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com.
📍 Where it livesAWS (NLB) + every node / pod
⚠ Watch outOne NLB per Service costs money — share one via Ingress/Gateway.

Headless Service

What it isA Service with clusterIP: None: no virtual IP, DNS returns pod IPs.
🎯 Why it existsClients sometimes need a specific pod (database primary, Kafka broker).
📄 What it looks like
clusterIP: None
⚙ What Kubernetes doesNo kube-proxy rules; CoreDNS returns one A record per Ready pod and per-pod names for StatefulSets.
📍 Where it livesDNS only
⚠ Watch outNo load balancing — the client decides.

ExternalName

What it isA Service type that is only a DNS alias (CNAME) to an outside host.
🎯 Why it existsGive external dependencies a cluster-local name you can repoint.
📄 What it looks like
type: ExternalName
externalName: api.checkout.com
⚙ What Kubernetes doesCoreDNS answers CNAME; nothing else is created. Before: provider host in config → After: payment-gateway-service.
📍 Where it livesDNS only
⚠ Watch outHostnames only (no IPs); TLS/Host still need the real name.

1.2Problems or needs — life without Services

Pods are cattle: they get new IPs, multiply, fail and live on a private network — calling them directly breaks in six ways.

!Six problems, step by step (no Service yet)

01Pod IPs change on every replacement
  • web calls menu-api by pod IP
  • the pod is replaced, rescheduled to node-2 with a new IP
  • web still dials the old IP → every call fails
Manual commands, in order
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=menu-api -o wide          # note IP 10.244.1.20
kubectl delete pod menu-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=menu-api -o wide          # new pod: 10.244.2.9
kubectl set env deployment/web-deployment MENU_API_URL=http://10.244.2.9:8080 -n jahez-prod   # manual fix, again
← BackStep 1 / 6
02No load balancing
  • three replicas, but the client holds one IP
  • one pod is overloaded, two are idle
  • every caller would need its own balancer
Manual commands, in order
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=menu-api -o wide
kubectl top pods -n jahez-prod -l app=menu-api   # 980m · 12m · 9m CPU
Step 2 / 6
03Scaling = editing every client
  • lunch peak: HPA scales menu-api 2 → 5
  • new pods get no traffic
  • every caller must be reconfigured and redeployed
Manual commands, in order
kubectl scale deployment/menu-api-deployment --replicas=5 -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=menu-api -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}'
kubectl set env deployment/web-deployment MENU_API_HOSTS=10.244.1.20,10.244.2.20,10.244.3.20,10.244.1.21,10.244.3.21 -n jahez-prod
kubectl set env deployment/cart-api-deployment MENU_API_HOSTS=… -n jahez-prod   # and every other caller
Step 3 / 6
04Cross-node routing is invisible but IPs still leak
  • pods on different nodes and subnets
  • the CNI routes it — reachable
  • but the caller still holds an IP that will change
Manual commands, in order
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -o wide   # NODE column
kubectl exec deploy/web-deployment -n jahez-prod -- curl -s http://10.244.2.20:8080/healthz
Step 4 / 6
05Unhealthy pods keep getting traffic
  • one replica fails its readiness probe
  • the client cannot tell and keeps calling it
  • ≈ one call in three fails
Manual commands, in order
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=menu-api   # READY 0/1 on one pod
kubectl describe pod menu-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-q8wzt -n jahez-prod | grep -A3 Readiness
Step 5 / 6
06Nothing outside can reach the pods
  • customers are on the internet
  • pod IPs are private and short-lived
  • the only workaround is a developer tunnel to one pod
Manual commands, in order
curl -m 5 http://10.244.1.10:3000/   # from a laptop: timeout
kubectl port-forward pod/web-deployment-5c8d7f9b4-h2m6p 3000:3000 -n jahez-prod   # one pod, dev only

→ How Kubernetes solves all six: 1.3 Solution.

Step 6 / 6Next →

1.3Solution — what a Service does

A Service puts a stable name and virtual IP in front of a label-selected set of Ready pods and makes every node forward connections to them.

The solution in steps

◆Anatomy of a Service — what really exists in the cluster

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Pods come and go — each with its own IP
Three menu-api replicas run on three nodes. Each pod gets an IP from its node's pod CIDR (10.244.1.0/24, 10.244.2.0/24, 10.244.3.0/24). Those IPs change whenever a pod is replaced, so web-1 cannot hard-code them.
← BackStep 1 / 8
02You create a Service → it gets a stable virtual IP
You apply menu-api-service. The API server gives it a ClusterIP from the service range (10.96.0.0/12): 10.96.0.50. No network card has this IP; rules on every node make it work (step 5).
Step 2 / 8
03The selector picks the pods
The Service says selector: app=menu-api. Every Ready pod with that label, on any node, becomes a backend. Labels decide membership, not IPs.
Step 3 / 8
04EndpointSlice: the live list of pod IPs
The EndpointSlice controller watches the pods and writes an EndpointSlice with the IP:port of every matching pod. When pods change, only this list changes; the Service and its ClusterIP stay the same.
Step 4 / 8
05kube-proxy programs every node
kube-proxy runs on every node. It watches Services and EndpointSlices and writes kernel rules: "packets to 10.96.0.50:80 → one of the 3 endpoints". Every node gets the same rules, so a pod on any node can use the Service.
Step 5 / 8
06CoreDNS gives it a name
CoreDNS also watches Services and answers menu-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local → 10.96.0.50. Pods in jahez-prod can just use menu-api-service.
Step 6 / 8
07A request uses all of it
① web-1 asks CoreDNS for menu-api-service and gets 10.96.0.50. ② It sends the packet to 10.96.0.50:80. ③ Before the packet leaves node-1, the kernel rewrites the destination (DNAT) to one real pod — here menu-api-3 on node-3.src 10.244.1.10:41022 → dst 10.96.0.50:80 DNAT ⇩ src 10.244.1.10:41022 → dst 10.244.3.20:8080
Step 7 / 8
08The four pieces of a Service
Service object (name, selector, ports, type) · ClusterIP (stable virtual IP) · EndpointSlice (live pod list) · kube-proxy rules + DNS record on every node. Every Service type adds entry points on top of these four.
Step 8 / 8Next →

What one apply creates (menu-api-service, 3 nodes)

Object / effectCountWho writes it
Service1you
ClusterIP1 (10.96.0.50)IP allocator
EndpointSlice1 with 3 endpointsEndpointSlice controller
iptables chains (KUBE-SVC + 3 × KUBE-SEP)4 per node × 3 nodeskube-proxy
DNS A record1CoreDNS

ProblemWhat fixes itField / objectDetails

Service types as layers

◆Service types as layers — one cluster, five behaviours

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01ClusterIP — internal only (default)
One virtual IP and DNS name, reachable only from inside the cluster. kube-proxy forwards to any matching pod on any node. A browser on the internet has no route to it.
← BackStep 1 / 6
02NodePort — + the same port on every node
Builds on ClusterIP and opens one port (30000–32767) on every node, here :30080. A request to any node IP on that port reaches the Service.
Step 2 / 6
03LoadBalancer — + a cloud load balancer
Builds on NodePort. A controller (the AWS Load Balancer Controller on EKS) creates an NLB that spreads traffic across the nodes or pods. Clients get one stable address on 80/443.
Step 3 / 6
04Headless — clusterIP: None
Not a separate type: a ClusterIP Service with no virtual IP. DNS returns the pod IPs and the client connects directly. Used with StatefulSets such as orders-db-stateful-set.
Step 4 / 6
05ExternalName — a DNS alias
No selector, no endpoints, no proxying. CoreDNS answers with a CNAME to an outside hostname, so pods use an internal name for an external dependency.
Step 5 / 6
06How they stack
Each external type adds an entry point on top of the one before — so a LoadBalancer Service also has a ClusterIP and NodePorts. Headless and ExternalName change how DNS answers instead.
Step 6 / 6Next →

Interactive: LoadBalancer vs NodePort

⚖LoadBalancer vs NodePort — side by side on one cluster

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Two ways in
Left: clients hit node IPs on the NodePort directly. Right: the same NodePorts sit behind an AWS NLB. Same cluster, same Service rules — the difference is what stands in front.
← BackStep 1 / 7
02❶ Ports
NodePort forces a high port into every URL. The LB listens on the standard ports.
Step 2 / 7
03❷ Entry points
NodePort exposes N node IPs that change with the node group. The LB gives one stable name.
Step 3 / 7
04❸ Health — node-2 dies
NodePort has no health checks: clients pointed at node-2 just fail. The LB health-checks every node and stops using node-2 within seconds.
Step 4 / 7
05❹ TLS
With an LB you terminate TLS once at the edge (an ACM certificate) instead of in every pod.
Step 5 / 7
06❺ Hops and client IP
Both depend on externalTrafficPolicy. With Local, LB health checks steer traffic only to nodes with a pod: no second hop and the client IP is kept.
Step 6 / 7
07Verdict
NodePort is a building block; LoadBalancer is the production front door on a cloud. To expose many HTTP services, put one LB in front of an Ingress or Gateway controller instead of one LB per Service.
Step 7 / 7Next →

Interactive: which type should I use?

?Decision walkthrough — which Service type? (Jahez examples)

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Start from the caller
The first question is not "which type is best" but who connects to it.
← BackStep 1 / 8
02Internal service-to-service → ClusterIP
Most Jahez services only talk to each other. ClusterIP gives a stable name + VIP and spreads calls across replicas.
Step 2 / 8
03Stateful, per-pod identity → Headless
When the client must pick a specific pod (primary vs replica, a Kafka broker, a Redis node), drop the VIP and let DNS return pod IPs.
Step 3 / 8
04Public traffic on a cloud → LoadBalancer
One managed LB with health checks and a stable address. In practice: one LB for the ingress/gateway controller, ClusterIP behind it.
Step 4 / 8
05No cloud LB → NodePort
Local clusters and bare metal. Fine for testing; for production put your own LB in front.
Step 5 / 8
06External dependency with a DNS name → ExternalName
Gives pods a cluster-local alias you can repoint later without code changes.
Step 6 / 8
07External dependency with only an IP → no selector
ExternalName cannot point at an IP. Create a Service without a selector and an EndpointSlice with the address.
Step 7 / 8
08Summary
Three questions cover almost every case. Everything else (traffic policies, affinity, ports) is tuning — see Part II.
Step 8 / 8Next →

When to choose something else

NeedUse instead / on topWhy
HTTP routing by host or path, one public LB for many servicesIngress or Gateway API (+ one LoadBalancer Service)a Service only knows IP:port
mTLS, retries, per-request balancing, canary by headerservice mesh (Istio, Linkerd)kube-proxy works per connection at L4
gRPC spread across pods without a meshHeadless Service + client-side round robinone HTTP/2 connection pins one pod
very large clusters, eBPF datapathCilium kube-proxy replacement or nftables modeiptables rule updates grow with Services
reach Services in another clusterAWS Cloud Map / MCS API, or an internal NLBClusterIPs are local to one cluster
limit who may call a ServiceNetworkPolicya Service never blocks traffic
2.Architecture and workflows

2.1Architecture — where each part runs

Services exist only as API objects; the control plane turns them into EndpointSlices, every node turns them into kernel rules, and CoreDNS turns them into names.

🏗Where every piece runs — the 3-node jahez-prod reference cluster

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Every diagram in this guide uses this cluster. Pods live on nodes; Services live nowhere — they are API objects that the control plane turns into DNS records and per-node kernel rules. (Pod names are shortened: menu-api-1 stands for a generated name such as menu-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp.)
ComponentRunsRole for Services
kube-apiserver + etcdEKS control planestores Services and EndpointSlices; allocates ClusterIPs and NodePorts
EndpointSlice controllerkube-controller-managerturns selector + pod readiness into EndpointSlices
AWS Load Balancer ControllerDeployment in kube-systemcreates NLBs for type LoadBalancer (loadBalancerClass service.k8s.io/nlb)
kube-proxyDaemonSet — every nodeprograms iptables/nftables: VIP → endpoints, NodePorts, health-check ports
CoreDNSDeployment in kube-system (kube-dns 10.96.0.10)answers Service names (A/AAAA/SRV, CNAME for ExternalName)
VPC CNIevery nodegives pods VPC IPs and routes pod-to-pod across nodes

2.2Repository layout — the jahez-prod Service manifests

Every Service in this guide lives in one Git folder per app; tap a file to open it, or a live object to see what the cluster made of it.
① GIT REPOSITORY · jahez-k8s
deploy/jahez-prod
web
menu-api
order-api
orders-db
observability
search
external
partners
② CLUSTER · namespace jahez-prod
👈 Tap any file or ⓘ to open it
YAMLdeploy/jahez-prod/web/web.yaml
The customer web app and its public NLB Service — every Service field in one file.
📄 web.yamlDeployment + Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/web:3.8.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 3000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: web
  annotations:
    # ⑤ Provider knobs (AWS Load Balancer Controller)
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
spec:
  # ① Which pods receive the traffic?
  selector:
    app: web
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - # ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land?
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  sessionAffinity: None
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
  # ④ What does DNS publish?
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
  # ⑤ Which cloud load balancer, and who may reach it?
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.io/nlb
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  # ⑥ Which IP families?
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
What each block does
  • ⑤ Provider knobs (AWS Load Balancer Controller) → service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme, service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type, spec
  • ① Which pods receive the traffic? → selector, app
  • ② How is it reached? → type, ports
  • ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land? → name, protocol, appProtocol, port, targetPort
  • ③ Where does the traffic go? → sessionAffinity, externalTrafficPolicy, internalTrafficPolicy, trafficDistribution
  • ④ What does DNS publish? → publishNotReadyAddresses
  • ⑤ Which cloud load balancer, and who may reach it? → loadBalancerClass, loadBalancerSourceRanges, allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts
  • ⑥ Which IP families? → ipFamilyPolicy, ipFamilies

Deep dive →

YAMLdeploy/jahez-prod/menu-api/menu-api.yaml
menu-api pods and the ClusterIP Service web and cart-api call.
📄 menu-api.yamlDeployment + Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-api                # ← the Service selector matches this label
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-api:1.14.2
          ports:
            - name: http             # ← targetPort: http points here
              containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:            # ← only Ready pods become endpoints
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          lifecycle:
            preStop:                 # ← drain before the endpoint is removed
              exec:
                command: ["sleep", "5"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-api-service           # DNS: menu-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
spec:
  # ① Which pods receive the traffic?
  selector:
    app: menu-api
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - # ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land?
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  sessionAffinity: None
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
  # ④ What does DNS publish?
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
  # ⑥ Which IP families?
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
What each block does
  • ① Which pods receive the traffic? → selector, app
  • ② How is it reached? → type, ports
  • ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land? → name, protocol, appProtocol, port, targetPort
  • ③ Where does the traffic go? → sessionAffinity, internalTrafficPolicy, trafficDistribution
  • ④ What does DNS publish? → publishNotReadyAddresses
  • ⑥ Which IP families? → ipFamilyPolicy, ipFamilies

YAMLdeploy/jahez-prod/order-api/order-api.yaml
order-api with two named ports (HTTP + gRPC) on one ClusterIP Service.
📄 order-api.yamlDeployment + Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-api:2.31.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
            - name: grpc
              containerPort: 9090
          readinessProbe:
            grpc:
              port: 9090
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② How is it reached? — two named ports
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - # ② REST for cart-api and web
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
    - # ② gRPC for rider-dispatch
      name: grpc
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: grpc
      port: 9090
      targetPort: grpc
  # ③ Where does the traffic go? — stay in the caller's zone when possible
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
What each block does
  • ① Which pods? → selector, app
  • ② How is it reached? — two named ports → type, ports
  • ② REST for cart-api and web → name, protocol, appProtocol, port, targetPort
  • ② gRPC for rider-dispatch → name, protocol, appProtocol, port, targetPort
  • ③ Where does the traffic go? — stay in the caller's zone when possible → trafficDistribution

YAMLdeploy/jahez-prod/orders-db/orders-db.yaml
PostgreSQL StatefulSet with a Headless Service for per-pod DNS names.
📄 orders-db.yamlSecret + Service + StatefulSet
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: orders-db-secret
  namespace: jahez-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  password: change-me-in-aws-secrets-manager
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  # ② How is it reached? — no virtual IP: DNS returns pod IPs
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
    - # ② PostgreSQL
      name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
  # ④ What does DNS publish? — Ready pods only
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-headless-service   # ← gives each pod a DNS name
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16.4
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: orders-db-secret
                  key: password
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 50Gi
What each block does
  • ① Which pods? → selector, app
  • ② How is it reached? — no virtual IP: DNS returns pod IPs → clusterIP, ports
  • ② PostgreSQL → name, port, targetPort
  • ④ What does DNS publish? — Ready pods only → publishNotReadyAddresses, apiVersion, kind, metadata, name, namespace

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: otel-agent-daemon-set

    matchLabels:

      tolerations:

apiVersion: v1

      port: 4317

Selector-less Service + hand-written EndpointSlice for the on-prem ERP.
📄 legacy-erp.yamlService + EndpointSlice
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: legacy-erp-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods? — none: no selector, you supply the endpoints
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - # ② clients call legacy-erp-service:8443
      name: https
      port: 8443
      targetPort: 8443
---
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: legacy-erp-endpoint-slice
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    # ① Which Service owns it?
    kubernetes.io/service-name: legacy-erp-service
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: platform-team
# ② What kind of address?
addressType: IPv4
# ③ Which ports? (names must match the Service port names)
ports:
  - name: https
    protocol: TCP
    port: 8443
# ④ Which endpoints, and can they take traffic?
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - "10.20.0.15"
    conditions:
      ready: true
What each block does
  • ① Which pods? — none: no selector, you supply the endpoints → —
  • ② How is it reached? → type, ports
  • ② clients call legacy-erp-service:8443 → name, port, targetPort, apiVersion, kind, metadata
  • ① Which Service owns it? → kubernetes.io/service-name, endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by
  • ② What kind of address? → addressType
  • ③ Which ports? (names must match the Service port names) → ports, name, protocol, port
  • ④ Which endpoints, and can they take traffic? → endpoints, addresses, conditions, ready

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service

    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert: arn:aws:acm:me-central-1:111122223333:certificate/1f2e3d4c-aaaa-bbbb-cccc-1234567890ab

  # ② How is it reached?

  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 185.10.20.0/24                 # Jahez office
    - 37.224.0.0/16                  # VPN egress
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false

2.3Internal order — what happens, in which order

Creating a Service is a chain of watches: API server → EndpointSlice controller → kube-proxy and CoreDNS (and the LB controller); afterwards the EndpointSlice keeps following the pods.

⇢From kubectl apply to the first packet

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01kubectl apply sends the object
The API server authenticates, authorizes, runs admission (defaults such as type: ClusterIP, sessionAffinity: None) and validates the spec.
← BackStep 1 / 8
02ClusterIP allocated, object stored
The IP allocator reserves 10.96.0.50 from the service range and the Service is written to etcd.
Step 2 / 8
03EndpointSlice controller builds the pod list
It sees the new Service, lists pods matching the selector and writes an EndpointSlice with each pod's IP, port and readiness.
Step 3 / 8
04kube-proxy on every node programs rules
Each node's kube-proxy gets the watch event and syncs its iptables/nftables rules (batched, usually within a second).
Step 4 / 8
05CoreDNS starts answering
CoreDNS's kubernetes plugin watches Services and serves the A record (and SRV records for named ports).
Step 5 / 8
06Only for type: LoadBalancer
The AWS Load Balancer Controller creates the NLB and writes its hostname into status.loadBalancer.ingress. Until then EXTERNAL-IP shows <pending>.
Step 6 / 8
07Traffic flows
A client resolves the name and connects to the ClusterIP; its own node's rules DNAT it to a pod.
Step 7 / 8
08Timing and takeaway
The Service exists the moment it is stored; it works once rules and DNS converge. Debug in that order: object → EndpointSlice → rules → DNS.
Step 8 / 8Next →

⟳EndpointSlices follow your pods

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Steady state
Three Ready pods → three endpoints → every node's rules split new connections three ways.
← BackStep 1 / 7
02menu-api-2 fails its readiness probe
The kubelet marks it not Ready; the EndpointSlice controller sets ready: false; kube-proxy on every node drops it. No restart, no Service change.
Step 2 / 7
03It recovers
The probe passes again → ready: true → back in rotation automatically.
Step 3 / 7
04Scale out: a 4th pod starts on node-3
HPA/KEDA adds menu-api-4 for the lunch peak. It is listed at once, but not ready, so it gets no traffic while it warms up.
Step 4 / 7
05menu-api-4 becomes Ready
Now four endpoints share the load — web changed nothing.
Step 5 / 7
06Rollout: menu-api-1 is terminating
The endpoint stays with terminating: true (and serving while it can still answer) but gets no new connections. A preStop sleep + graceful shutdown let in-flight requests finish.
Step 6 / 7
07Through all of it
The replacement pod joins the slice. The ClusterIP and DNS name never changed — only the EndpointSlice did.
Step 7 / 7Next →

2.4Workflows — one real request per type

Each type traced end to end on the same 3-node cluster: DNS, the node rules, the hop, the reply.

ClusterIP

▶ClusterIP · cart-api-1 → order-api-service:80 (full lifecycle)

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01cart-api-1 wants to place an order
The app only knows a name: http://order-api-service/orders. It never sees an order-api pod IP.
← BackStep 1 / 7
02DNS query to CoreDNS
The pod's /etc/resolv.conf says nameserver 10.96.0.10 (the kube-dns Service) with search domains jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local …. The query lands on the coredns pod on node-3.QNAME order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local QTYPE A
Step 2 / 7
03DNS answer: the ClusterIP
CoreDNS answers with the Service IP, not a pod IP.order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local. 30 IN A 10.96.0.100
Step 3 / 7
04SYN to the virtual IP
The packet leaves cart-api-1 through its veth and enters node-1's netfilter (PREROUTING → KUBE-SERVICES). The rule for 10.96.0.100:80 matches.src 10.244.1.40:51544 → dst 10.96.0.100:80 [SYN]
Step 4 / 7
05DNAT to a real endpoint
The rule picks one endpoint at random and rewrites the destination. This connection got order-api-1 on the same node, so the packet never leaves node-1.dst 10.96.0.100:80 ⇒ dst 10.244.1.41:8080
Step 5 / 7
06The reply looks like it came from the Service
conntrack remembers the rewrite and reverses it on the reply, so the app sees an answer from 10.96.0.100:80.
Step 6 / 7
07The next connection may go anywhere
Each new connection is balanced separately — this one goes to order-api-3 on node-3. The cart-api code is identical either way.
Step 7 / 7Next →

▶ClusterIP · same-node vs cross-node path

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01web-1 calls menu-api-service
It sends to the ClusterIP 10.96.0.50:80. From here on everything happens in the kernel of the sending node.
← BackStep 1 / 6
02node-1's rules match the Service
kube-proxy wrote the same chain on every node. The jump probabilities give each of the 3 endpoints an equal share of new connections.
Step 2 / 6
03Case A — endpoint on the same node
DNAT picks menu-api-1. The packet goes pod → host → pod without touching the network.
Step 3 / 6
04Case B — endpoint on another node
DNAT picks menu-api-2. The rewritten packet (destination = pod IP) is routed to node-2.
Step 4 / 6
05node-2 simply delivers it
Service translation happens once, at the source node. node-2 sees an ordinary pod-to-pod packet.
Step 5 / 6
06The reply is un-NATed where it started
The response returns to node-1, conntrack swaps the source back to 10.96.0.50:80, and web-1 never learns which pod answered.
Step 6 / 6Next →

▶ClusterIP · how traffic is spread across replicas

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Connection 1 → order-api-1
The first random pick lands on the local pod.
← BackStep 1 / 5
02Connection 2 → order-api-2
A new TCP connection is a new pick — this one lands on node-2.
Step 2 / 5
03Connection 3 → order-api-3
Over many connections the three pods get about equal shares.
Step 3 / 5
04Why "equal": the probabilities
iptables tests rules in order: 1/3 for the first endpoint, then 1/2 of the rest, then the remainder — 1/3 each. (nftables/IPVS modes use their own algorithms.)
Step 4 / 5
05Trap: balancing is per connection, not per request
kube-proxy only sees new TCP connections. A long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connection pins every request to one pod. Fix it client-side (gRPC round-robin over a Headless Service) or with a mesh/L7 proxy.
Step 5 / 5Next →

NodePort

▶NodePort · browser → node-1:30080 → local web pod

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Browser → node-1 on port 30080
Any node IP works; here the user points at node-1 (192.168.1.101).
← BackStep 1 / 5
02node-1 matches the NodePort rule
kube-proxy opened 30080 on every node with iptables rules (no process listens). The NodePort chain jumps into the same Service chain the ClusterIP uses.
Step 2 / 5
03DNAT to a web pod
The pick is web-1 on node-1 itself. With the default externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster the source is also SNAT'd to the node IP so the reply comes back through node-1.
Step 3 / 5
04The pod serves the request
nginx on :3000 answers. It logs the node IP as the client — the real client IP is lost with Cluster.
Step 4 / 5
05Response back to the browser
conntrack undoes the SNAT and DNAT; the browser sees a reply from 192.168.1.101:30080.
Step 5 / 5Next →

▶NodePort · request hits node-3, pod lives on node-1

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Browser → node-3:30080
node-3 has no web pod — but the NodePort is open there too.
← BackStep 1 / 5
02node-3 picks an endpoint on another node
Its Service chain lists every web pod in the cluster. It DNATs to web-1 on node-1 and SNATs the source to node-3's IP.
Step 2 / 5
03Extra hop, client IP hidden
The packet crosses node-3 → node-1. Because of the SNAT, nginx logs 192.168.1.103 instead of the customer's IP.
Step 3 / 5
04Reply goes back the same way
The pod answers node-3 (the SNAT address); node-3 reverses the NAT and replies to the browser.
Step 4 / 5
05The trade-off you control
externalTrafficPolicy: Local removes the hop and keeps the client IP, but a node without a local pod drops the traffic. See 3.12.
Step 5 / 5Next →

LoadBalancer

▶LoadBalancer · provisioning and request lifecycle

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01You apply type: LoadBalancer
Kubernetes first does everything a NodePort Service does: allocate ClusterIP 10.96.0.20 and NodePort 30080 on every node.
← BackStep 1 / 7
02The controller provisions the LB
On EKS the AWS Load Balancer Controller creates an NLB and writes its hostname into status.loadBalancer.ingress.
Step 2 / 7
03Targets register and pass health checks
In instance mode the NLB targets every node on :30080. (In IP mode it targets pod IPs directly and skips the NodePort hop — see 3.18.)
Step 3 / 7
04Client → one stable address
The browser resolves jahez.net to the NLB and connects on port 80. No node IPs or high ports are exposed.
Step 4 / 7
05NLB → a node → kube-proxy → a pod
The NLB picks node-2. From there it is the NodePort path: iptables DNATs to a web pod (local or remote).
Step 5 / 7
06Response path
The reply is un-NATed on node-2 and returned through the NLB.
Step 6 / 7
07Health checks + traffic policy
With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, each node answers the LB health check only when it has a ready local pod, so the LB skips node-3.
Step 7 / 7Next →

Headless

👻Headless + StatefulSet → a stable DNS name per pod

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
In the diagrams orders-db-0 is short for the real pod name orders-db-stateful-set-0.

▶Headless · write to the primary, read from the replica

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01order-api-1 needs to write
Writes must go to the primary, pod 0. A ClusterIP Service would pick a random pod — so we address the pod by name.
← BackStep 1 / 8
02DNS: per-pod record
CoreDNS answers orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local with that pod's own IP.
Step 2 / 8
03Direct TCP to the primary
There is no virtual IP, so kube-proxy wrote no rules for this Service. The packet goes straight to 10.244.1.30:5432.
Step 3 / 8
04Primary replicates to the replica
PostgreSQL streams WAL from pod 0 to pod 1 (node-1 → node-2), also by stable DNS name.
Step 4 / 8
05order-api-2 needs to read
Reads can go to the replica to offload the primary.
Step 5 / 8
06DNS: a different pod name
Changing -0 to -1 in the hostname changes which pod you get: 10.244.2.30.
Step 6 / 8
07Direct read, same node
order-api-2 and the replica share node-2, so the query never leaves the node.
Step 7 / 8
08Read/write split achieved
Stable per-pod names are what StatefulSets + Headless Services are for: databases, Kafka brokers, Elasticsearch nodes, Redis replicas.
Step 8 / 8Next →

▶Headless · discover all pods with one DNS query

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01Query the bare Service name
Instead of one pod, ask for orders-db-headless-service itself.
← BackStep 1 / 5
02DNS query to CoreDNS
Same resolver path as any Service lookup.
Step 2 / 5
03One A record per Ready pod
Without a ClusterIP, CoreDNS returns every Ready endpoint's IP (plus SRV records for named ports).
Step 3 / 5
04The client decides
Load balancing, failover or "connect to all" is now application logic — Kubernetes no longer chooses for you.
Step 4 / 5
05Where this is used
Peer discovery for clustered systems and client-side balancing for long-lived gRPC connections.
Step 5 / 5Next →

ExternalName

▶ExternalName · order-api-2 → payment-gateway-service → api.checkout.com

↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
01order-api-2 calls payment-gateway-service
The code uses an internal name. Which provider sits behind it is decided by the Service YAML, not the app.
← BackStep 1 / 6
02Normal DNS query to CoreDNS
Same resolver path as for any Service.
Step 2 / 6
03CoreDNS answers with a CNAME
Not an A record: payment-gateway-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local CNAME api.checkout.com.
Step 3 / 6
04The name is resolved outside the cluster
CoreDNS forwards api.checkout.com upstream (the VPC resolver) and returns the public A record.
Step 4 / 6
05The pod connects directly
No proxying, no port mapping — the pod opens TLS straight to the provider through the node's egress (NAT gateway).
Step 5 / 6
06Trap: HTTP Host and TLS
Only DNS is aliased. HTTP Host headers and TLS SNI still need the real hostname, or HTTPS fails with a certificate mismatch.
Step 6 / 6Next →
Part II

Low Level

Details and depth — the object reference

3.Service

3.0How a Service works

A Service is a namespaced API object that gives a changing set of pods one stable name and virtual IP, and tells every node how to forward traffic to them.

You write the what (which pods, which ports, how it is reached); Kubernetes writes the how (a ClusterIP, an EndpointSlice, kernel rules on every node, a DNS record, maybe a cloud LB). The Service lives as long as you keep it — pods behind it can be replaced any number of times.

Familycore/v1 · networking
Scopenamespaced (jahez-prod)
Survivespod restarts, rollouts, scaling
Typical usestable name for a set of pods

The logic, read first

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which pods receive the traffic?selectormembership by label, never by IP
② How is it reached?type · clusterIP · portsthe address: VIP, node port, cloud LB or DNS alias
③ Where does the traffic go?sessionAffinity · externalTrafficPolicy · internalTrafficPolicy · trafficDistributionrouting rules once a packet arrives
④ What does DNS publish?publishNotReadyAddresses · externalNamethe cluster phone-book entry
⑤ Which cloud LB, and who may reach it?loadBalancerClass · loadBalancerSourceRanges · allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts · annotationsthe outside door
⑥ Which IP families?ipFamilyPolicy · ipFamiliesIPv4, IPv6 or both
★ Written by KubernetesclusterIP(s) · nodePort · healthCheckNodePort · statusnever write these by hand

Structure

Service
├─ metadata      name · namespace · labels · annotations (⑤)
├─ spec
│  ├─ ① selector
│  ├─ ② type · clusterIP · ports[ name · protocol · appProtocol · port · targetPort · nodePort ]
│  ├─ ③ sessionAffinity(+Config) · externalTrafficPolicy · internalTrafficPolicy · trafficDistribution
│  ├─ ④ publishNotReadyAddresses · externalName
│  ├─ ⑤ loadBalancerClass · loadBalancerSourceRanges · allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts
│  └─ ⑥ ipFamilyPolicy · ipFamilies
└─ status        loadBalancer.ingress (★)

Full YAML — every field, grouped by question

📄 web.yamlDeployment + Service · every Service field in one file
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/web:3.8.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 3000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: web
  annotations:
    # ⑤ Provider knobs (AWS Load Balancer Controller)
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
spec:
  # ① Which pods receive the traffic?
  selector:
    app: web
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - # ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land?
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  sessionAffinity: None
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
  # ④ What does DNS publish?
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
  # ⑤ Which cloud load balancer, and who may reach it?
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.io/nlb
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  # ⑥ Which IP families?
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4

Every property — tap to open

🌳 Service fields — tap a field
① Which pods receive the traffic?group
selectorobjectlabels a pod must ALL have to become an endpoint
Equality-only map (AND). Matches pods in the same namespace. Only Ready pods receive traffic. Omit it and Kubernetes manages no endpoints — you write EndpointSlices yourself.
ValueMeaning
app: menu-apievery Ready pod labelled app=menu-api
(omitted)no managed endpoints — selector-less Service
Default: none
Deep dive →
② How is it reached?group
typestringwhich entry points Kubernetes builds
Each external type includes the ones below it: LoadBalancer ⊃ NodePort ⊃ ClusterIP. ExternalName is a DNS alias only.
ValueMeaning
ClusterIPvirtual IP + DNS, inside the cluster
NodePort+ port 30000–32767 on every node
LoadBalancer+ cloud load balancer
ExternalNameCNAME to an outside host
Default: ClusterIP
Deep dive →
clusterIPstringthe virtual IP — allocated, pinned, or None (headless)
Immutable after creation. Omit it to get one from the service range. None creates a Headless Service: no VIP, no kube-proxy rules, DNS returns pod IPs.
ValueMeaning
(omitted)allocated, e.g. 10.96.0.50
10.96.0.10requested IP — fails if taken or outside the range
Noneheadless
Default: allocated
Deep dive →
portslistthe ports the Service exposes
One entry per port. Every entry needs a unique name when there are two or more.
Deep dive →
namestringport name — required with 2+ ports; creates SRV records
Deep dive →
protocolstringTCP · UDP · SCTP
Default: TCP
Deep dive →
appProtocolstringL7 hint for gateways and meshes (http, http2, grpc, kubernetes.io/h2c)
Deep dive →
portintegerrequiredthe port clients dial on the Service
Any port 1–65535. Clients never see the container port.
Default: —
Deep dive →
targetPortint | stringwhere the packet lands on the pod
A number, or the name of a containerPort. A name lets pods change their port without touching the Service.
ValueMeaning
8080pod port 8080
httpwhatever the pod calls "http"
Default: same as port
Deep dive →
nodePortintegerport opened on every node (NodePort / LoadBalancer)
Range 30000–32767 by default. Omit it and the API server picks a free one.
ValueMeaning
30080pinned
(omitted)random, e.g. 31847
Default: random free port
Deep dive →
③ Where does the traffic go?group
sessionAffinitystringsticky routing by client IP
With ClientIP every new connection from the same source IP goes to the same pod until it has been idle for timeoutSeconds.
ValueMeaning
Nonebalance every connection
ClientIPsame source IP → same pod
Default: None
Deep dive →
sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSecondsintegerstickiness idle timeout (1–86400)
Default: 10800 (3 h)
Deep dive →
externalTrafficPolicystringmay external traffic hop to another node?
Cluster: any node forwards to any pod and SNATs. Local: only local pods, client IP preserved; nodes without a pod fail the LB health check.
ValueMeaning
Clustereven spread, client IP lost
Localno hop, client IP kept, needs evenly spread pods
Default: Cluster
Deep dive →
healthCheckNodePortintegerhealth-check port the LB probes when Local (written for you)
Deep dive →
internalTrafficPolicystringkeep in-cluster traffic on the caller's node?
Local uses only endpoints on the same node and drops traffic when there are none.
ValueMeaning
Clusterall endpoints
Localsame-node endpoints only
Default: Cluster
Deep dive →
trafficDistributionstringprefer nearby endpoints, fall back when needed
A preference, not a rule. Never drops traffic.
ValueMeaning
PreferSameZonesame zone first (PreferClose = alias)
PreferSameNodesame node first (v1.34+)
Default: unset
Deep dive →
④ What does DNS publish?group
publishNotReadyAddressesbooleanpublish pods in DNS before they are Ready
For peer discovery during bootstrap (Elasticsearch, Kafka, etcd). Keep false on client-facing Services.
ValueMeaning
falseReady pods only
trueall pods
Default: false
Deep dive →
externalNamestringCNAME target for type ExternalName
Must be a DNS name; IPs are not valid CNAME targets.
Deep dive →
⑤ Which cloud load balancer, and who may reach it?group
loadBalancerClassstringwhich controller implements the LB (immutable)
ValueMeaning
service.k8s.io/nlbAWS Load Balancer Controller
Default: cluster default
Deep dive →
loadBalancerSourceRangeslistclient CIDRs allowed at the LB
Default: open to all
Deep dive →
allocateLoadBalancerNodePortsbooleanalso allocate NodePorts? false for IP-target LBs
Default: true
Deep dive →
metadata.annotationsmapprovider knobs: scheme, target type, TLS cert, cross-zone
Deep dive →

Default: SingleStack
Deep dive →

clusterIPslistone IP per family on dual-stack clusters (written for you)

① Which pods?

3.1selector — which pods are the backends

The selector is a set of labels; every Ready pod in the same namespace that has all of them becomes an endpoint of the Service.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which pods count?selectora label filter evaluated all the time
Which of them get traffic?pod readinessonly Ready pods
What if there is no selector?(omitted) + EndpointSliceyou supply the addresses
📄 menu-api.yamlDeployment + Service · Deployment + Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-api                # ← the Service selector matches this label
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-api:1.14.2
          ports:
            - name: http             # ← targetPort: http points here
              containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:            # ← only Ready pods become endpoints
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          lifecycle:
            preStop:                 # ← drain before the endpoint is removed
              exec:
                command: ["sleep", "5"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-api-service           # DNS: menu-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
spec:
  # ① Which pods receive the traffic?
  selector:
    app: menu-api
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - # ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land?
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  sessionAffinity: None
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
  # ④ What does DNS publish?
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
  # ⑥ Which IP families?
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4

▶ selector — matching, mismatching, none

selector:
  app: menu-api

Pods on all three nodes carry app=menu-api; all three IPs land in the EndpointSlice and every node's rules include them.

The Service resolves in DNS but has no endpoints. This is the most common Service bug.

② How is it reached?

3.2type — which entry points you get

type decides how many layers of entry point Kubernetes builds: a virtual IP, plus a port on every node, plus a cloud load balancer — or just a DNS alias.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Reachable only inside the cluster?ClusterIPinternal VIP + DNS
Also on every node?NodePort+ :30000–32767 on each node
Also through a cloud LB?LoadBalancer+ NLB in front
Is it outside the cluster?ExternalNameCNAME only
One section per type follows: 3.3 ClusterIP · 3.4 NodePort · 3.5 LoadBalancer · 3.6 ExternalName · 3.7 Headless.
🌳 Property tree — tap a field
typestringwhich entry points Kubernetes builds
Each external type includes the ones below it: LoadBalancer ⊃ NodePort ⊃ ClusterIP. ExternalName is a DNS alias only.
ValueMeaning
ClusterIPvirtual IP + DNS, inside the cluster
NodePort+ port 30000–32767 on every node
LoadBalancer+ cloud load balancer
ExternalNameCNAME to an outside host
Default: ClusterIP
Deep dive →

Deep dive — values compared

▶ type — what each value builds

type: ClusterIP   # default
Internal only

Virtual IP + DNS record; every node DNATs to a pod. Nothing outside the cluster can reach it.

← Back1 / 5
type: NodePort
+ a port on every node

Everything ClusterIP does, plus the same port on every node — even nodes without a pod.

2 / 5
type: LoadBalancer
+ an external load balancer

Everything NodePort does, plus a controller creates a cloud LB and writes its address to status.

3 / 5
type: ExternalName
externalName: api.checkout.com
A DNS alias

No selector, endpoints, ClusterIP or kube-proxy rules. CoreDNS returns a CNAME.

4 / 5
typeClusterIPNodePortExternal LBReachable fromDNS answer
ClusterIP✓——clusterA → VIP
NodePort✓✓—anything that reaches a nodeA → VIP
LoadBalancer✓✓ (unless disabled)✓internet / VPCA → VIP
ExternalName———n/aCNAME
Headless———clusterA → pod IPs

3.3Type · ClusterIP

ClusterIP gives the Service a virtual IP that only exists inside the cluster; any pod can call it and kube-proxy forwards each new connection to one Ready pod.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Who can call it?type: ClusterIPpods and nodes inside the cluster
Which address?clusterIPa VIP from 10.96.0.0/12 — on no network card
How is load spread?kube-proxy rulesrandom pick per new TCP connection

How ClusterIP works — step by step

#What happensWhere
1cart-api calls http://order-api-service/orders — a name, no IPapp code
2DNS query to 10.96.0.10 (kube-dns) for order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.localpod resolver → CoreDNS
3CoreDNS answers the ClusterIP 10.96.0.100CoreDNS
4SYN to 10.96.0.100:80 enters the node's netfilter (PREROUTING → KUBE-SERVICES)node kernel
5DNAT to one order-api pod IP:8080, chosen at randomnode kernel
6same node: delivered via veth · other node: routed by the VPC CNInetwork
7reply is un-NATed by conntrack, so the client sees 10.96.0.100node kernel

Real-world examples

Caller → ServiceWhy ClusterIP
cart-api → order-api-service:80internal call; order-api scales 3 → 8 at lunch with zero client change
web → menu-api-service:80the browser never talks to menu-api directly; web proxies it
rider-dispatch → order-api-service:9090 (gRPC)second named port on the same Service — see 3.10
📄 order-api.yamlDeployment + Service · Deployment + ClusterIP Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-api:2.31.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
            - name: grpc
              containerPort: 9090
          readinessProbe:
            grpc:
              port: 9090
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② How is it reached? — two named ports
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - # ② REST for cart-api and web
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
    - # ② gRPC for rider-dispatch
      name: grpc
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: grpc
      port: 9090
      targetPort: grpc
  # ③ Where does the traffic go? — stay in the caller's zone when possible
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone

3.4Type · NodePort

NodePort keeps everything ClusterIP does and also opens one port (30000–32767) on every node, so anything that can reach a node IP can reach the Service.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which port on the nodes?ports[].nodePortsame number on every node
Which nodes answer?all of themeven nodes without a pod
Keep the client IP?externalTrafficPolicyCluster hides it, Local keeps it

How NodePort works — step by step

#What happens
1client → 192.168.1.103:30080 (any node)
2node rule KUBE-NODEPORTS matches 30080 → jumps into the Service chain
3DNAT to a web pod (maybe on another node) + SNAT to the node IP (policy Cluster)
4pod answers the node; node un-NATs and replies to the client
📄 web-nodeport-service.yamlService · NodePort Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-nodeport-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods?
  selector:
    app: web
  # ② How is it reached? — the same port on every node
  type: NodePort
  ports:
    - # ② client → node:30080 → Service :80 → pod :http (3000)
      name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
      nodePort: 30080
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster

3.5Type · LoadBalancer

LoadBalancer keeps everything NodePort does and asks a controller to create a cloud load balancer in front of the nodes (or straight to the pods).
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Who builds the LB?loadBalancerClassAWS Load Balancer Controller on EKS
Public or VPC-only? TLS?annotationsprovider knobs
Who may connect?loadBalancerSourceRangesCIDR allow-list
Nodes or pods as targets?allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts + target-typeinstance vs ip mode

How LoadBalancer works — step by step

#What happens
1apply → ClusterIP + NodePort allocated (unless disabled)
2controller creates the NLB, target group and security group
3targets register (nodes:NodePort or pod IPs) and pass health checks
4controller writes the NLB hostname to status → EXTERNAL-IP
5client → NLB → node/pod → (kube-proxy) → pod
6delete → finalizer makes the controller remove the NLB first
📄 partner-admin-service.yamlService · LoadBalancer Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: partner-admin-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    # ⑤ Provider knobs
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert: arn:aws:acm:me-central-1:111122223333:certificate/1f2e3d4c-aaaa-bbbb-cccc-1234567890ab
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports: "443"
spec:
  # ① Which pods?
  selector:
    app: partner-admin
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - name: https
      port: 443
      targetPort: 8443
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  # ⑤ Which cloud load balancer, and who may reach it?
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.io/nlb
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 185.10.20.0/24                 # Jahez office
    - 37.224.0.0/16                  # VPN egress
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false

3.6Type · ExternalName (+ externalName)

ExternalName makes a Service name a DNS alias (CNAME) for a host outside the cluster — no IP, no endpoints, no proxying.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
What does the name point to?externalNamea DNS name, never an IP
What about ports?portsinformational only — not remapped

How ExternalName works — step by step

#What happens
1order-api resolves payment-gateway-service
2CoreDNS answers CNAME api.checkout.com.
3the resolver follows the CNAME upstream (VPC resolver) → public IP
4the pod connects directly through the NAT gateway

3.7clusterIP — allocated, pinned, or None (Headless)

clusterIP is the Service's virtual IP; omit it to get one, pin it for bootstrap infrastructure, or set None to make a Headless Service whose DNS returns pod IPs.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Do I need a VIP at all?clusterIP: NoneHeadless: client picks the pod
Must it be a known address?clusterIP: 10.96.0.10pinned (rare)
Per-pod names?StatefulSet serviceNamepod-N.service-name

How Headless works — step by step

#What happens
1app asks DNS for orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local
2CoreDNS returns the pod IP (10.244.1.30) — no VIP
3TCP goes straight to the pod: no kube-proxy rules exist for this Service
4asking for the bare Service name returns one A record per Ready pod
5reads/writes split by pod name: -0 primary, -1 replica

Real-world examples

WorkloadHeadless use
orders-db PostgreSQLwrites → pod 0 (primary), reads → pod 1 (replica)
Kafka / Elasticsearchbrokers and nodes discover each other by name
menu-api gRPC clientsmenu-api-headless-service + client-side round robin across all pods
📄 orders-db.yamlSecret + Service + StatefulSet · Secret + Headless Service + StatefulSet
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: orders-db-secret
  namespace: jahez-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  password: change-me-in-aws-secrets-manager
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  # ② How is it reached? — no virtual IP: DNS returns pod IPs
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
    - # ② PostgreSQL
      name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
  # ④ What does DNS publish? — Ready pods only
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-headless-service   # ← gives each pod a DNS name
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16.4
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: orders-db-secret
                  key: password
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 50Gi

3.8ports[].port & targetPort

📄 menu-api.yamlDeployment + Service · Deployment + Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-api                # ← the Service selector matches this label
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: menu-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-api:1.14.2
          ports:
            - name: http             # ← targetPort: http points here
              containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:            # ← only Ready pods become endpoints
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          lifecycle:
            preStop:                 # ← drain before the endpoint is removed
              exec:
                command: ["sleep", "5"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-api-service           # DNS: menu-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
spec:
  # ① Which pods receive the traffic?
  selector:
    app: menu-api
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - # ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land?
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  sessionAffinity: None
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
  # ④ What does DNS publish?
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
  # ⑥ Which IP families?
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4

③ Where does the traffic go?

3.11sessionAffinity + sessionAffinityConfig

With ClientIP, kube-proxy sends every new connection from the same source IP to the same pod until the client has been idle for timeoutSeconds.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Sticky or not?sessionAffinityNone or ClientIP
For how long?sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSecondsidle timeout, default 10800 s
📄 report-export-service.yamlService · ClientIP affinity
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: report-export-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods?
  selector:
    app: report-export
  # ② How is it reached?
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  # ③ Where does the traffic go? — same client IP → same pod
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 1800

sessionAffinitystringsticky routing by client IP

3.12externalTrafficPolicy (+ healthCheckNodePort)

Cluster lets a node forward external traffic to a pod on any node (and SNATs it); Local only uses pods on the same node, keeps the client IP, and makes nodes without a pod fail the LB health check.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
May traffic hop to another node?externalTrafficPolicyCluster yes · Local no
How does the LB know?healthCheckNodePortper-node health endpoint (Local only)
📄 web.yamlDeployment + Service · externalTrafficPolicy: Local
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/web:3.8.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 3000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: web
  annotations:
    # ⑤ Provider knobs (AWS Load Balancer Controller)
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
spec:
  # ① Which pods receive the traffic?
  selector:
    app: web
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - # ② Which port do clients use, and where does it land?
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
  # ③ Where does the traffic go?
  sessionAffinity: None
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone
  # ④ What does DNS publish?
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
  # ⑤ Which cloud load balancer, and who may reach it?
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.io/nlb
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  # ⑥ Which IP families?
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4

4.EndpointSlice

4.0How an EndpointSlice works

An EndpointSlice is the live list of pod addresses behind a Service — written by a controller from the selector and pod readiness, read by kube-proxy and CoreDNS.

You rarely write one. The EndpointSlice controller creates one or more per Service (up to 100 endpoints each) and updates them whenever pods start, stop or change readiness. The older Endpoints API is deprecated since v1.33.

Familydiscovery.k8s.io/v1
Scopenamespaced
Survivesuntil its Service is deleted
Typical usedebug "why no traffic?"

The logic, read first

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which Service owns it?kubernetes.io/service-name labelthe link to the Service
② What kind of address?addressTypeIPv4 / IPv6
③ Which ports?portsresolved pod ports by name
④ Which endpoints, and can they take traffic?endpoints[] · conditions · zone · hintsthe address book with health flags
★ Written by the controllerownerReferences · managed-bybookkeeping
🖨 kubectl get endpointslice -n jahez-prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=menu-api-service -o yamlexample output

kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:

ready = serving and not terminating. kube-proxy sends new connections to ready endpoints; when none are ready it may fall back to serving + terminating ones.
ValueMeaning

serving: true, terminating: truedraining — used only if nothing is ready
ready: false, serving: falsefailing readiness — no traffic

4.1Endpoint conditions — ready · serving · terminating

Three flags per endpoint decide whether it gets new connections: ready (yes), serving + terminating (only as a last resort while draining), not serving (no).

▶ conditions — one state per tab

conditions:
  ready: true
  serving: true
  terminating: false
Normal

Readiness probe passes; the endpoint is in every node's rules.

← Back1 / 4
ready: false
serving: false
Failing readiness

The pod keeps running (readiness ≠ liveness) but gets no traffic until the probe passes.

2 / 4
ready: false
serving: true
terminating: true
Draining during a rollout

No new connections while other endpoints are ready; existing connections finish. Add a preStop sleep so kube-proxy on every node has removed the endpoint before the app stops.

3 / 4
readyservingterminatingNew connections?
truetruefalseyes
falsefalsefalseno
falsetruetrueonly if no ready endpoint exists
4 / 4Next →
Watch the conditions change during readiness failures, scale-out and rollouts in EndpointSlices follow your pods (2.3).

4.2Hand-written EndpointSlices (Service without selector)

For a backend that is not a pod — an on-prem system or a fixed IP — create a Service without a selector and write the EndpointSlice yourself.
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which Service?kubernetes.io/service-name: legacy-erp-servicethe link
④ Which addresses?endpoints[].addressesthe external IP
📄 legacy-erp.yamlService + EndpointSlice · Service + EndpointSlice
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: legacy-erp-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which pods? — none: no selector, you supply the endpoints
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - # ② clients call legacy-erp-service:8443
      name: https
      port: 8443
      targetPort: 8443
---
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: legacy-erp-endpoint-slice
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    # ① Which Service owns it?
    kubernetes.io/service-name: legacy-erp-service
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: platform-team
# ② What kind of address?
addressType: IPv4
# ③ Which ports? (names must match the Service port names)
ports:
  - name: https
    protocol: TCP
    port: 8443
# ④ Which endpoints, and can they take traffic?
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - "10.20.0.15"
    conditions:
      ready: true

5.Internals

5.1DNS records a Service creates

CoreDNS turns every Service into DNS records — an A record to the ClusterIP, pod IPs for Headless, a CNAME for ExternalName, SRV records for named ports.
RecordNameAnswer
A (ClusterIP)menu-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local10.96.0.50
A (Headless)orders-db-headless-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.localone per Ready pod: 10.244.1.30, 10.244.2.30
A (StatefulSet pod)orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local10.244.1.30
SRV (named port)_grpc._tcp.order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local0 100 9090 order-api-service…
CNAME (ExternalName)payment-gateway-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.localapi.checkout.com.

Pod resolv.conf

# /etc/resolv.conf inside any jahez-prod pod (written by the kubelet)
nameserver 10.96.0.10
search jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local me-central-1.compute.internal
options ndots:5

ndots:5 — a name with fewer than five dots is tried with each search domain first. menu-api-service resolves on the first try; api.checkout.com (2 dots) is tried four times before the real name. Add a trailing dot (api.checkout.com.) in hot paths to skip that.

⌘ Commands
kubectl run tmp -n jahez-prod --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- dig +search menu-api-service
A record through the search list

5.2kube-proxy rules — the iptables chains

kube-proxy turns each Service and its endpoints into NAT chains on every node: match the VIP, pick an endpoint at random, DNAT to it.
🖨 sudo iptables-save -t nat | grep menu-api-service (on any node)example output
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.96.0.50/32 -p tcp -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/menu-api-service:http cluster IP" -m tcp --dport 80 -j KUBE-SVC-MENU
-A KUBE-SVC-MENU -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/menu-api-service:http -> 10.244.1.20:8080" -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.33333333349 -j KUBE-SEP-AAA
-A KUBE-SVC-MENU -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/menu-api-service:http -> 10.244.2.20:8080" -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.50000000000 -j KUBE-SEP-BBB
-A KUBE-SVC-MENU -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/menu-api-service:http -> 10.244.3.20:8080" -j KUBE-SEP-CCC
-A KUBE-SEP-AAA -p tcp -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/menu-api-service:http" -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 10.244.1.20:8080
-A KUBE-NODEPORTS -p tcp -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/web-nodeport-service:http" -m tcp --dport 30080 -j KUBE-EXT-WEB
-A KUBE-EXT-WEB -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ        # policy Cluster → SNAT
-A KUBE-EXT-WEB -j KUBE-SVC-WEB

Chain names are hashes in reality (KUBE-SVC-ABCD1234…); they are shortened here. Headless and ExternalName Services produce no rules.

⌘ Commands (on a node)
sudo iptables-save -t nat | grep menu-api-service
the rules for one Service (iptables mode)
sudo — shell command
sudo nft list table ip kube-proxy | grep 10.96.0.50
the same in nftables mode
sudo — shell command
sudo conntrack -L -d 10.96.0.50
live NAT entries for the VIP
sudo — shell command

5.3kube-proxy modes

kube-proxy can program the kernel in different ways; iptables is the Linux default, nftables is its successor, IPVS is deprecated.
ModeStatusHow it worksWhen
iptablesdefault on LinuxNAT chains with random-probability jumpsmost clusters (EKS default)
nftablesGA since v1.33maps and sets: near-constant lookups, incremental updates; kernel 5.13+large clusters, new builds
IPVSdeprecated in v1.35kernel L4 balancer with algorithms (rr, lc, sh…)migrate to nftables
userspaceremovedkube-proxy proxied every connection itselfnever
eBPF replacementCNI featuree.g. Cilium kube-proxy replacementwhen your CNI owns Service routing
⌘ Commands
kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy-config -o yaml | grep mode
which mode EKS configured (empty = iptables)
send to API server
kubectl -n — -n
-o — output format (wide, yaml, json, jsonpath=…, name)

6.1kubectl apply -f

kubectl apply -f

create or update objects from YAML — the normal way to manage Services

apply sends your YAML to the API server, which creates the Service or merges your changes into the live one.
kubectl apply -f menu-api.yaml

kubectl apply — create or update from YAML
-f — file (or folder / URL) with the YAML
Output
deployment.apps/menu-api-deployment unchanged

the Service matches the file; controllers update EndpointSlices, kube-proxy rules and DNS within seconds.
changing an immutable field (clusterIP, loadBalancerClass) → "field is immutable": delete and recreate instead.
Template
kubectl apply -f <FILE|DIR|URL> [-n <NS>] [--dry-run=server] [--server-side] [-R]
Parameters
ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
-frequiredfile, folder or URL with YAMLmenu-api.yaml
deploy/jahez-prod/menu-api/		kubectl apply -f menu-api.yaml
-nnamespace for objects without onejahez-prodkubectl apply -f menu-api.yaml -n jahez-prod
--dry-run=servervalidate with the API server, save nothingserver
client		kubectl apply -f menu-api.yaml --dry-run=server
--server-sideserver-side apply (field ownership)(no value)kubectl apply -f menu-api.yaml --server-side
-Rrecurse into sub-folders(no value)kubectl apply -R -f deploy/jahez-prod/
Watch out
  • apply never deletes fields you removed from other managers' ownership — use the same tool every time (GitOps or kubectl, not both).
  • a folder apply creates objects in file order; Services before Deployments avoids a moment with no endpoints only if both exist anyway — order rarely matters.

kubectl expose deployment menu-api-deployment --name=menu-api-service --port=80 --target-port=http -n jahez-prod --dry-run=client -o yaml > menu-api-service.yaml

6.3kubectl create service

kubectl create service

create a Service of a given type from flags

create service builds a Service from flags — clusterip, nodeport, loadbalancer or externalname — without needing an existing workload.
kubectl create service clusterip menu-api-service --tcp=80:8080 -n jahez-prod --dry-run=client -o yaml
build object from flags → print YAML locally · nothing sent — cluster unchanged
kubectl create — create a new object
--tcp=80:8080 — port[:targetPort] pair for the Service
-n — namespace to work in

-o — output format (wide, yaml, json, jsonpath=…, name)

nodeport

6.11Troubleshooting — follow the packet

Debug in the order the request travels: DNS → Service → EndpointSlice → node rules → pod; each red number is a stage that raises a real error.

3Endpoints: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=…selector ≠ pod labels; pods not Ready (readiness probe); wrong namespace
